newsitem.title: USA: US Airways to buy back shares from British Airways.
newsitem.headline: US Airways to buy back shares from British Airways.

text.p: US Airways Group Inc., bringing a turbulent four-year relationship with British Airways Plc closer to an end, said Tuesday it will buy most of its preferred stock held by the British airline, giving itself a financial boost.

Analysts said US Airways' plan to buy back the preferred shares for about $126.2 million will reduce its fully diluted shares outstanding, cut its preferred dividend payments by $27 million a year and still leave the company with a cushion of more than $700 million in free cash flow.

"It's very positive," Helane Becker, an airline analyst with Smith Barney, said. "This was a big issue, a question of whether they'd be able to do it. We're pleased that they will buy back the shares."
SBC Warburg airline analyst Timothy Ross said the stock repurchase was another sign that US Airways, which used to be called US Air, was succeeding in its turnaround.

"They are very healthy. They are still highly leveraged, but they are coming around to the industry average," Ross said. "It's a combination of improved profitability and capital spending constraints. They've been pretty tight with their spending."
US Airways, which has some of the highest costs in the airline industry, faces intense competition at home, especially from low-cost regional carriers.
It recently announced plans to eliminate unprofitable routes, consolidate facilities and reduce its fleet. The airline also plans to lay off 103 of its 5,000 pilots July 1.
Analysts also expect the carrier to cut additional routes.
In addition, as its relationship with British Airways nears an end, US Airways will be left without a major international partner at a time when its rivals are strengthening their global alliances.
The two airlines began feuding publicly last summer after British Air proposed a broad alliance with American Airlines, which is owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp.

US Airways sued British Airways in July, alleging that the deal with American undermined US Airways' relationship with the British carrier and could create a monopoly on the key trans-Atlantic route between the United States and Britain.

Then in December British Airways, which invested about $400 million in US Airways in 1993, said it planned to sell its 24.6 percent stake in its U.S. marketing partner. The three British Airways representatives on US Airways' board resigned in January.

Arlington, Va.-based US Airways said in February that it would not exercise its right to buy back British Airways' stake, but it changed tack Tuesday, saying it can now meet the capital surplus requirements to repurchase them.

A Delaware law limits share repurchases unless a company meets certain capital surplus thresholds. The airline, which is incorporated in Delaware, declined to provide details on its capital surplus position.

"We see this as a very attractive opportunity to purchase stock at a discount to current markets," US Airways Chairman Stephen Wolf said. "We will continue to seek opportunities to use the company's resources to increase value for our shareholders."

US Airways said it will repurchase and retire most of the preferred stock held by the British carrier. British Airways agreed to convert the remaining preferred stock it holds into common stock in June.
Analysts expect that British Airways will be forced to sell its remaining 14 percent stake in US Airways before British Airways' proposed alliance with American Airlines is approved.

It is expected to sell its remaining stake in a series of privately negotiated block transactions once the preferred shares are converted into US Airways common stock on or before June 3, analysts said.
A British Airways spokesman declined to comment.
Analysts said the stock repurchase would not affect the lawsuit, which is still pending. US Airways would not comment on the lawsuit.
US Airways stock added $2 to $37.175 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.
